en: All eighteen elements are established in sixfold groups, consisting of the bases, the objects, and those dependent upon them, for the sake of dispelling the delusion regarding mind and form. Here, among the sense-bases (*āyatanas*), the mind is included as a single base by virtue of its status as the subject that possesses objects.
Because they arise from two types of bases, there are seven elements; however, the mind-element is sixfold.
(2.36) Yet, within these four—namely, the desire realm and so forth—all of them are present;
thus, there are fourteen, three, and eight, due to the corruption by desire for sense-pleasures and the rest. (2.37)
The realm of desire consists of ten states; the form realm has fifteen aspects;
the formless realm has four natures; and the stainless is the untainted, which is threefold.
There are seven stations of consciousness due to the mind’s attachment to them.

By way of being the appropriator, the four [aggregates] are devoid of mind. (5.39) For consciousness, through the relishing of feeling regarding form, is enticed by perceptions and, supported by volitional formations, persists. (6.40)

Because they delight in dwelling in the seven states of non-perception and at the peak of existence, these are not designated as abodes of beings; nor are the miserable realms designated as such because of the torment of suffering.
These include the denizens of hell, along with animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans.
Some destinies are indeterminate; those designated as aggregates are with outflows. The intermediate state is said to be that which leads to them, and it exists in five ways.
Because there is no going to a place to be gone to, it does not arise in the formless realms.
One enters, remains, and departs with full awareness; one does not depart [unaware]. One remains unaware in all three cases of entering the womb.
There are four modes of birth: gods and hell-beings are born by transformation (*aupapāduka*).
Pretas are also born from the womb; humans and animals are of four types.

(11 [45]) The five contaminated aggregates, determined by their distinct states, are momentary and twofold: that which is called "existence" (bhava), consisting of the destruction of karma and the subsequent arising [of a new state]. (12 [46])
In the same realm, from a defiled state of a similar category, a defiled state arises;
likewise, from a non-defiled state, a non-defiled state arises at the junctions of existences (*pratisandhi*). Existence (*bhava*) is held to consist of either five or four members.

And for others, there is no single constituent part as appropriate within the three realms of existence. The realms of desire and form consist of five aggregates; the formless realm consists of four aggregates due to the absence of form. Alternatively, existence is threefold by way of karma. (14–15)

That which is the arising of afflictions, karma, and the bases from delusion and so forth is dependent origination, characterized by arising in dependence. (16) That by whose power, by what means, in what manner, for whom, and wherein there is projection—
That by whose power, that by which, how its production occurs, what its end is, and how it is—this twelvefold cycle, with three sections and two joints, is the driver;
it exists as a relationship of cause and effect, remaining complete in its fullness. (17–18)
Dharma is the adversary of knowledge; ignorance and all other impurities are its opposites.
Because they are conjoined, it is not due to defilement that the intellect has non-manifestation as its characteristic.
(19 [53]) The formative forces of body, speech, and mind, tainted karma, and views—

The fourth aggregate is the nutriments, as well as the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). All phenomena that are formless are called "name" (*nāman*), so it is said, because they bend (*namana*). Other than that, the division of letters is "name," which is the basis for the activity of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). (20–21)
Visible form (*rūpa*), however, consists of color and shape, because it is defined by sight in some cases;
the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is called "form" in other cases, because it is the basis for the most excellent forms.
(22 [56]) In this context, the five factors beginning with discernment (*vidā*), ending with mental attention (*manasikāra*), constitute "name" (*nāma*).

Form is said to be so called because of its susceptibility to transformation; it consists of whatever is derived from the primary elements or composed of them. (23) Contact is the conjunction of these three; it is the basis for verbal designation and resistance.
From the duality of knowledge and ignorance, there is one [category]; [the aggregates] consist of five, one, and six respectively. (24)
From the three types of feeling, craving arises in three ways; from that, it becomes fivefold.
Attachment, the grasping for sense-pleasures and so forth, thus constitutes the existence of karma.
[This pertains to] earth, water, fire, air, space, and the mind associated with outflows.
The state of being an element (*dhātu*) is due to their supporting the production of form, mental factors, and so forth.

(26) The internal [elements] consist of femininity, masculinity, vitality, the five sensations, faith and the others, the three untainted [faculties], and the triad beginning with "I shall come to know the unknown. (27)
For the purpose of grasping objects, through the distinction between eunuchs, women, and men;
for the sake of maintaining the continuum, life-force, and sensations; from the side of the afflictions;
from the side of liberation—there are five, three, and [one] according to the distinction of levels. (28 [62])
The faculties are the intellect and three; the female and male faculties are separate from the body. (29) Six are of three kinds; eight are wholesome; eight are neutral.
Fourteen, ten, three, and thirteen [faculties] exist within the [eighteen] elements. (30)
Eight are not mental factors, while thirteen are indeed mental factors;
one is mind alone, seven are material, and none are entirely karma.
Or, they say seven are born of karma; eight are to be cultivated in every way. (31 [65])
Neither one nor eight parts, nor even six, can indeed be obtained.
For the kavaḍīkārāhāra consists of odor and so forth, as well as contaminated contact and mental volition; it is called "support" because it sustains the mind. (32–33)
All [beings] in the desire realm, three in the form realm, and up to one in the arising of happiness;
one is beyond that—such is the individual distinction among those in the hells and other states.
For the falling away of beings occurs both from the exhaustion of their lifespan and from the exhaustion of their merit.
Through the destruction of both, as well as for others through the destruction of one or the other, and for yet others through the destruction of neither.
(35 [69]) The Compendium of Elements is completed. Laru.
